patient.chief_complaint: Sudden severe headache while at rest, 'different from my usual migraines'
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Patterson is a 52-year-old woman with a history of migraines who presents with a sudden onset headache that began approximately 4 hours before arrival. She describes it as entirely different from her usual migraines: onset was instantaneous, peaked within seconds, and was rated 10/10 in severity. Her typical migraines build over 20-30 minutes and are unilateral with nausea. This headache was bilateral, global, and accompanied by a brief sensation of losing consciousness that resolved within 30 seconds. She then vomited twice and called 911. She was told by paramedics she was briefly confused but she denies loss of consciousness. On arrival, headache persists at 7/10. She has had no similar severe acute headaches before. She reports mild neck stiffness. She uses sumatriptan for migraines but has not had a typical migraine in 6 months. Given her migraine history, she initially dismissed the headache, delaying her call for help by approximately 2 hours. She denies fever, focal weakness, visual loss, or rash. She has had no recent illness, trauma, or viral prodrome.

results.finding: Any thunderclap headache requires CT ± LP to exclude SAH regardless of migraine history
Age >40, neck pain/stiffness, witnessed LOC, onset with exertion - any 1 requires workup
CT sensitivity 98-100% within 6 hours; LP required if CT negative and presentation <6 hours

output.summary: Any sudden-onset severe ('thunderclap') headache requires non-contrast CT head and lumbar puncture if CT is negative or late presentation. The Ottawa SAH decision rule identifies high-risk features requiring workup. LP with spectrophotometry is the gold standard for CT-negative presentations. History of migraine does not modify these diagnostic criteria.

output.impression: 1. Post-coiling assessment: complete aneurysm occlusion (Raymond class I) at right MCA bifurcation. 2. No residual aneurysm filling. 3. Parent MCA and M2 branches patent. Follow-up DSA at 6 months recommended.

key_reasoning_points: A thunderclap headache (maximum severity at onset, <1 minute to peak) is SAH until proven otherwise regardless of migraine history
Migraine history is a red herring in this case that delayed diagnosis by 2 hours
LP demonstrating non-clearing bloody CSF with xanthochromia on spectrophotometry is definitive for SAH
Sumatriptan is absolutely contraindicated in SAH due to vasoconstrictive properties that could exacerbate cerebral vasospasm
The subtle CT findings (Fisher 2, thin Sylvian blood) explain why the diagnosis was not immediately apparent
Right MCA aneurysm location correlates with right Sylvian fissure blood distribution

red_herrings.data_point: Known history of migraines (well-controlled for 5 years on propranolol) with patient self-attributing the headache to migraine and delaying emergency call by 2 hours
red_herrings.intended_effect: Migraine history creates strong anchoring bias — both the patient and clinicians may attribute the thunderclap headache to an atypical migraine episode, delaying or forgoing SAH workup
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Migraine history does NOT reduce the likelihood of SAH when a headache is thunderclap (maximum severity at onset, <1 minute to peak). The Ottawa SAH Rule does not exclude patients with migraine history. Key discriminator: this headache was bilateral, global, and instantaneous — entirely different from her typical unilateral migraines that build over 20-30 minutes. Any thunderclap headache requires CT ± LP regardless of migraine history.

red_herrings.data_point: Sumatriptan in patient's medication list — patient asking to use it for pain management
red_herrings.intended_effect: The clinician or patient may consider using sumatriptan (as part of the migraine management reflex) without recognizing it is absolutely contraindicated in SAH
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Sumatriptan is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in confirmed SAH — its vasoconstrictive properties could exacerbate cerebral vasospasm and provoke delayed cerebral ischemia. Additionally, sumatriptan + sertraline (current medication) carries serotonin syndrome risk. IV acetaminophen or opioids are the appropriate analgesics in confirmed SAH.
